opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting gaps in current AI systems. Language models have read basically everything humans have ever written about the physical world, and yet they'll still happily tell you something that any three-year-old would know is impossible: that you can fit a couch through a mail slot, or that a ball rolls uphill on its own. The reason is that language is a very lossy, low-bandwidth description of a fundamentally three-dimensional, continuous world. We as humans don't learn physics from reading about it; we learn it from moving through space, picking things up, dropping them, seeing objects from different viewpoints. The text is almost an afterthought layered on top of that.

So the way I think about it is that spatial intelligence needs to be its own first-class capability, not something you hope emerges from scaling next-token prediction on text. You want models whose internal representation is actually grounded in 3D structure: geometry, occlusion, physical extent, how things persist when you look away. If a model really represents the world as a 3D space with objects that have shape and size, then a lot of these physical impossibilities become obvious almost for free, because the representation itself won't let you put a large thing inside a small thing.

That's a big part of why we've been working on world models at World Labs: models that can generate and reason about full 3D environments you can move through, rather than just flat pixels or tokens. Pixels are a step closer than text, but even 2D video models can drift and violate consistency, because they're not forced to maintain a coherent 3D world underneath. When you build in that 3D structure, you get consistency across viewpoints and over time, and that's the substrate where physical common sense can actually live.

Longer term, I don't think it's language models versus spatial models. It's about combining them. Language is incredibly good for abstraction, planning, communicating intent. Spatial models are good at grounding all of that in a world that actually obeys geometry and physics. Hooking those together, where the language side can query or imagine in a real 3D representation, is how I think you get systems that find physical impossibilities as obvious as we do.

r001.rationale: It says humans learn through moving, handling objects, and seeing viewpoints, then argues that spatial intelligence requires an internal representation grounded in 3D structure, geometry, and object size.

r002.rationale: It discusses combining language and spatial models, but does not ask how difficult it would be to distill spatial understanding from world models into a language model.

r003.rationale: It says the goal is not language models versus spatial models, but does not ask whether spatial intelligence requires abandoning language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that I'm not sure you can get there by starting from the language model and bolting spatial reasoning onto it. Language is this incredibly lossy, compressed description of the world. If I say "the cup is on the table," there's a huge amount I haven't told you: where on the table, how big the cup is, whether it's about to tip over. Humans fill all that in effortlessly because we have this underlying 3D model of the scene that we're reasoning over, and the words are just pointers into it.

So when a language model sees a picture of a person standing on a ceiling, or a chair with a leg that passes through a wall, the reason it doesn't flinch is that it never built the scene. It learned a very good statistical model of what captions look like next to pixels, and that correlation can get you surprisingly far, but there's no geometry underneath. There's nothing in there that knows that objects occupy volume and two volumes can't overlap, or that gravity points down and unsupported things fall.

The way I think about it is that spatial intelligence is really a separate pillar from linguistic intelligence. It evolved first, it's older, and most animals have a lot of it without having any language at all. So the research program I'm most excited about is: can we train models directly on the structure of the 3D world? Generate it, reconstruct it, predict how it changes when you act in it. If a model can take a bunch of images and produce a consistent 3D representation of the scene, then a physical impossibility isn't something you need to explain to it in words. It just falls out, because the thing it's trying to build doesn't close. The reconstruction has a contradiction in it, the same way it does in your head when you look at an Escher drawing.

And then the interesting part is connecting those two systems. Once you have a model that has an actual internal representation of space, language becomes a really useful interface to it. You can ask "could that shelf hold that box" and the answer comes from reasoning over geometry rather than from a sentence that sounded right in the training data. I think that's where this goes: not language models that happen to know about space, but world models that happen to speak.

r001.rationale: It says humans effortlessly fill in missing details because they reason over an underlying 3D model of the scene.

r002.rationale: It discusses connecting spatial and language systems, but does not ask how difficult it would be to distill spatial understanding from world models into a language model.

r003.rationale: It argues for world models that can speak, but does not ask whether spatial intelligence requires abandoning language models.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is what kind of experience you need to develop that intuition. For us, physical impossibilities feel obvious, but we’ve spent our entire lives seeing things move, manipulating objects, and learning what happens when we take an action. A language model gets a very different kind of experience. It can learn descriptions of those things, but that doesn’t necessarily give it a consistent understanding of space.

One way to push on this is to train models to predict how a scene changes over time, especially in response to an action. If I push this object, where does it go? What happens when it reaches the edge of the table? That forces you to confront things that a static image or a verbal description can leave ambiguous.

But predicting a plausible-looking video isn’t quite the same as understanding the underlying situation. You’d want to test whether the model stays consistent when you change the viewpoint or ask it to reason through a different action. To me, that’s the central challenge: getting from something that looks right to an understanding that holds up across those changes.

r001.rationale: The response says humans learn from seeing motion and manipulating objects, but it does not explain that they map encounters onto an internal three-dimensional representation.

r002.rationale: It discusses training models to predict scene changes, but does not ask how difficult it would be to distill spatial understanding from world models into a language model.

r003.rationale: It does not ask whether spatial intelligence requires abandoning language models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that spatial intelligence isn’t just knowing facts about the world. It’s being able to imagine a situation and reason about what would happen if you changed it. If I tell you to put a large object through a small opening, you can almost immediately see why that won’t work. You don’t necessarily translate it into a verbal argument first.

Language gives us a lot of information about those things, but it’s an indirect signal. I think we want models that can learn from seeing the world, seeing things move, and ultimately taking actions and observing the consequences. Then the question is whether they’ve learned a representation that supports prediction: if I push this, where does it go? If I move this object, what becomes visible?

And we have to be careful about how we measure that. A model describing an image convincingly doesn’t necessarily mean it understands the geometry. You want to change the viewpoint or the arrangement and see whether its answers remain consistent. That’s a much stronger test of whether it has something like a spatial understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says people can imagine a situation and see why an object will not fit, but it does not explain this as mapping experience onto an internal three-dimensional representation.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning from the world and building predictive representations, but does not ask how difficult it would be to distill spatial understanding from world models into a language model.

r003.rationale: It does not ask whether spatial intelligence requires abandoning language models.
